stemMd:
Regional librarian: Across the region, the branch libraries that extended their opening hours into the evening lent 12 percent more items in the following year than they had in the year before. Extending opening hours into the evening therefore causes a library's lending to rise.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the librarian's argument?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Lending was flat the year before at the branches that later extended their hours, and comparable branches that never did stayed flat in both years.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The 12 percent figure was measured, for each branch, over the twelve months immediately following the date its evening hours began.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The branches that extended their evening hours held larger and more recently updated collections, on average, than the branches that did not.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Most items borrowed during the new evening hours were borrowed by regular patrons who had previously done their borrowing during the day.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The branches that extended their evening hours also enlarged their acquisitions budgets and bought many new titles in the same year.

explanationMd:
A causal conclusion drawn from a before-and-after comparison is exposed on two flanks. The rise might continue a trend already under way at those branches (they were growing anyway), or it might reflect something that lifted lending at libraries generally that year, whether or not they changed their hours. A strengthener is any fact that closes one of those flanks.

The choice saying lending was flat the year before at the branches that later extended their hours, and that comparable branches that never did stayed flat in both years, closes both at once. "Flat the year before at the branches that later extended their hours" kills the pre-existing-trend story: these branches were not already climbing. "Comparable branches that never did stayed flat in both years" supplies a control group over the same two years: in the very year the extending branches lent 12 percent more, comparable libraries that made no change saw no rise, so whatever produced the 12 percent was not something happening to libraries generally that year. A flat prior year at the comparison branches would not be enough on its own; what matters is that they stayed flat while the extending branches rose. That is as close to a controlled comparison as an observational claim of this kind can get, and it is what makes that choice decisively the best answer.

Check your work by asking, for each choice, which way the argument moves once the fact is added.

- The choice about the twelve-month measurement window is a definition of the measurement window. It tells you what was counted, not why it rose, and every rival explanation fits it equally well.
- The choice about larger and more recently updated collections at the extending branches says those branches differed systematically from the others before the change. That is a selection problem and a rival source of higher lending, so the argument gets *weaker*.
- The choice about most evening borrowers being regular patrons who had previously borrowed by day suggests borrowing was merely rescheduled from daytime to evening, which is consistent with total lending not being driven up by the change at all — weaker again.
- The choice about enlarged acquisitions budgets and many new titles introduces a rival cause operating at exactly the same time — weaker still.

The habit worth keeping: on a strengthen question for a causal claim, look first for a choice that rules out an alternative explanation or supplies a comparison group, and be suspicious of any choice that adds a second thing that changed at the same time.

distractorRationale.b: This merely specifies the measurement window and adds no evidence about causation. Every explanation of the rise, including a pre-existing trend or a region-wide surge, is equally compatible with the figure being measured over the twelve months after each branch's evening hours began. A fact that no rival hypothesis would contest cannot discriminate between hypotheses.
distractorRationale.c: This states that the two groups of branches differed before the change, which is the selection problem the argument most needs to escape. Larger and fresher collections are an obvious alternative source of higher lending, so the choice supplies a confound rather than eliminating one.
distractorRationale.d: If the evening borrowers are mostly regular patrons who used to borrow in the daytime, the evening figures may represent lending moved rather than lending created, which puts pressure on the claim that the extension raised total lending. This is a weakener dressed in the vocabulary of the new evening hours.
distractorRationale.e: A larger acquisitions budget and a wave of new titles are a rival explanation for the rise in lending, operating in the same branches in the same year. Adding them makes the causal conclusion harder to sustain, not easier. It is tempting because it names a plausible driver of library use, but a strengthener must remove competitors rather than introduce one.

accessibilityText: A short causal argument. Branch libraries that extended opening hours into the evening lent 12 percent more items in the following year than in the year before, and the librarian concludes that extending evening hours causes lending to rise. The question asks which statement, if true, most strengthens the argument. Five answer choices follow: a statement about lending at the extending branches and at comparable branches across both years, the measurement window for the 12 percent figure, the larger collections at the extending branches, the regular patrons who moved their borrowing to the evening, and the enlarged acquisitions budgets. No notation, tables or figures appear.

provenance.notes: Original stimulus and choices. Strengthen item on a before-and-after causal claim; the key supplies both a flat pre-trend and an untreated comparison group, while two distractors are weakeners and two are inert. Not derived from any published LSAT item.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The argument infers causation from a before/after rise at the branches that extended their hours. Its main weaknesses are a pre-existing upward trend and a region-wide rise that would have happened anyway. The choice saying lending was flat beforehand and that comparable branches without evening hours stayed flat rules out both, which makes it the strongest. The choice tying the 12 percent window to the date each branch's evening hours began only confirms that the rise came after the change, so it helps much less. The choice about larger, newer collections describes levels rather than changes, so it is neutral at best and could suggest a confound. The choices about regular patrons shifting from daytime borrowing and about enlarged acquisitions budgets both weaken the argument: one suggests borrowing was moved rather than added, and the other offers a different cause. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue2-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: The argument infers causation from a before/after rise at branches that extended their hours, so it is open to two objections: lending may already have been rising at those branches, or it may have risen everywhere. The choice saying lending was flat at those branches the year before, and that comparable branches that never extended stayed flat, answers both objections at once and isolates the change in hours. The choice about measuring over the twelve months after evening hours began only restates the timing the stimulus already gives and rules out no alternative cause. The choices about larger, newer collections and about bigger acquisitions budgets in the same year offer other explanations, so they weaken the argument. The choice about regular patrons moving their borrowing from day to evening suggests displacement rather than new lending, which at best does nothing for the conclusion and at worst weakens it.]
